newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian gold seen slow as investors focus on stocks.
newsitem.headline: Asian gold seen slow as investors focus on stocks.

text.p: As the world's stock markets soar and money flows into equities, Asian gold dealers expect gold prices to languish in a narrow range in the coming week.
"People are more interested in equities right now," F.Y. Wong, a director at Rothschild Ltd in Hong Kong, said on Friday.
Gold prices have been trapped between US$380 and $383 an ounce as investors have turned their attention to the red-hot bourses of Hong Kong, New York, and London.
And dealers throughout the region say that is where prices will stay next week as steady physical demand is more than matched by selling.
"Demand is there, but in general the market is painfully slow," a trader with a European bullion house in Singapore said.
Seasonal demand in India -- which picks up after the monsoon and peaks during Diwali, or Hindu new year, in early November, has not been as high as expected this year, dealers said.
The lower festival demand had kept prices tight, dealers in Bombay said, adding that fresh arrivals had pushed prices down by five rupees per 10 grams in Thursday trading.
"Seasonal buyers are keeping away as they expect the customs department to resume the sale of illegal gold it has seized," a dealer in Bombay told Reuters.
The price of a gold biscuit (116.5 gram) fell 50 rupees to 60,200 rupees (US$1,689).
The market's weakness has led to layoffs at some Hong Kong banks and bullion houses, industry sources said, with expensive senior staff being replaced in some cases.
"The industry is suffering from the lack of interest," one industry source said on condition of anonymity.

"The cost of doing business is very high in Hong Kong with the rents and salaries here, and a lot of banks and bullion houses are looking at their bottom lines in a climate of high cost and low return," he said.
Asian traders predicted demand in the region should gradually pick up towards the end of October and said physical demand was still healthy.
"We're seeing bits and pieces of demand, but it's more than matched by professional selling," one trader in Singapore said.
"We're seeing some selling by the Japanese and I heard that Australian sellers may be in the market," another said.
Much of the gold that moves through Singapore goes to India, while Hong Kong supplies other major Asian markets.
Traders based in Singapore said the price there was locked between $381 and $383 an ounce.
"If the market closes above $383, it's a selling opportunity for people here," a dealer said. Rothschild's Wong, meanwhile, said $378 an ounce was the magic number in Hong Kong.
"There's been some short covering and fund buying," he said.
"At the $382-$383 level (on Wednesday) there was some producer selling and profit-taking which took the price back down a little bit.

"The range will continue to be tight. I don't see any strong uptake. Producers are always waiting in the wings and the possibility that the IMF (International Monetary Fund) will sell some of its gold will hang over the market until there is some decisive move there," he said.
The IMF has put off until 1997 a decision on whether to sell five million ounces of gold to benefit the world's poor.

Singapore gold premiums were steady at 30-40 U.S. cents an ounce in the absence of fresh news in the market, dealers said. Silver provided the only encouraging note in the precious metals market after remaining firm above $5.
